questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 1.2
questions.subject: Programming and DS
questions.questionHtml:
An $n \times n$ array $v$ is defined as follows:

$v\left[i,j\right] = i - j$ for all $i, j, i \leq n, 1 \leq j \leq n$

The sum of the elements of the array $v$ is

  1. $0$
  2. $n-1$
  3. $n^2 - 3n +2$
  4. $n^2 \frac{\left(n+1\right)}{2}$

review.independentCheck: Skew-symmetric matrix sum: sum(i-j) over all 1<=i,j<=n equals 0 by algebraic decomposition and off-diagonal cancellation. Matches official key A.
review.notes: Skew-symmetric matrix sum: sum(i-j) over all 1<=i,j<=n equals 0 by algebraic decomposition and off-diagonal cancellation. Matches official key A.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 1.4
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.questionHtml:
Let $S$ and $T$ be languages over $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$ represented by the regular expressions $(a+b^*)^*$ and $(a+b)^*$, respectively. Which of the following is true?

  1. $S \subset T$
  2. $T \subset S$
  3. $S = T$
  4. $S \cap T = \phi$

review.independentCheck: Both (a+b*)* and (a+b)* generate Sigma* = {a, b}*, proving language equality S = T. Matches official key C.
review.notes: Both (a+b*)* and (a+b)* generate Sigma* = {a, b}*, proving language equality S = T. Matches official key C.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 1.5
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.questionHtml:
Let $L$ denote the languages generated by the grammar $S \to 0S0 \mid 00$.
Which of the following is TRUE?

  1. $L = 0^+$
  2. $L$ is regular but not $0^+$
  3. $L$ is context free but not regular
  4. $L$ is not context free

review.independentCheck: Grammar S -> 0S0 | 00 generates positive even powers of 0, L = (00)+, which is recognized by a 3-state DFA and excludes odd lengths, so L is regular but not 0+. Matches official key B.
review.notes: Grammar S -> 0S0 | 00 generates positive even powers of 0, L = (00)+, which is recognized by a 3-state DFA and excludes odd lengths, so L is regular but not 0+. Matches official key B.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 1.8
questions.subject: CO & Architecture
questions.questionHtml:
Comparing the time T1 taken for a single instruction on a pipelined CPU with time T2 taken on a non-pipelined but identical CPU, we can say that

  1. T1 ≤ T2
  2. T1 ≥ T2
  3. T1 < T2
  4. T1 and T2 plus the time taken for one instruction fetch cycle

review.independentCheck: Single instruction latency on pipelined CPU T1 = k * (max(tau_i) + d) >= sum(tau_i) = T2 due to latch overhead and slowest stage clocking. Matches official key B.
review.notes: Single instruction latency on pipelined CPU T1 = k * (max(tau_i) + d) >= sum(tau_i) = T2 due to latch overhead and slowest stage clocking. Matches official key B.

questions.subject: Other / Optional
questions.questionHtml:
The 8085 microprocessor responds to the presence of an interrupt

  3. by checking the TRAP pin for 'high' status at the end of the execution of each instruction.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 1.10
questions.subject: CO & Architecture
questions.questionHtml:
The most appropriate matching for the following pairs$$\begin{array}{ll} \text{X: Indirect addressing} & \text{1: Loops } \\  \text{Y: Immediate addressing } & \text{2: Pointers} \\   \text{Z: Auto decrement addressing } & \text{3: Constants } \\  \end{array}$$ is

  1. $X - 3,  Y - 2,  Z - 1$
  2. $X - 1,  Y - 3,  Z - 2$
  3. $X - 2,  Y - 3,  Z - 1$
  4. $X - 3,  Y - 1,  Z - 2$

review.independentCheck: Indirect addressing matches pointers (X-2), immediate addressing matches constants (Y-3), auto-decrement matches loops (Z-1). Matches official key C.
review.notes: Indirect addressing matches pointers (X-2), immediate addressing matches constants (Y-3), auto-decrement matches loops (Z-1). Matches official key C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 1.11
questions.subject: Programming in C
questions.questionHtml:
The following C declarations:

struct node { 
    int i:
    float j;
 };
 struct node *s[10];

define s to be:

  1. An array, each element of which is a pointer to a structure of type node
  2. A structure of $2$ fields, each field being a pointer to an array of $10$ elements
  3. A structure of $3$ fields: an integer, a float, and an array of $10$ elements
  4. An array, each element of which is a structure of type node

review.independentCheck: In struct node *s[10], array operator [] has higher precedence than *, making s an array of 10 pointers to struct node. Matches official key A.
review.notes: In struct node *s[10], array operator [] has higher precedence than *, making s an array of 10 pointers to struct node. Matches official key A.

questions.subject: Programming in C
questions.questionHtml:
The most appropriate matching for the following pairs$$\begin{array}{|ll|ll|}\hline X: & \text{m = malloc(5); m = NULL;} & 1: & \text{using dangling pointers} \\\hline  Y: & \text{free(n); n -> value = 5;} & 2: & \text{using uninitialized pointers} \\\hline   Z: & \text{char *p , *p = ‘a’ ; } & 3:  & \text{lost memory} \\\hline \end{array}$$ is:

  1. $X - 1 \ \  Y - 3 \ \  Z - 2$
  2. $X - 2 \ \  Y - 1 \ \  Z - 3$
  3. $X - 3 \ \  Y - 2 \ \  Z - 1$
  4. $X - 3 \ \  Y - 1 \ \ Z - 2$

review.independentCheck: Lost memory (X-3), dangling pointer (Y-1), uninitialized pointer (Z-2). Matches official key D.
review.notes: Lost memory (X-3), dangling pointer (Y-1), uninitialized pointer (Z-2). Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 1.14
questions.subject: Programming and DS
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following nested representation of binary trees: $(X \ Y \ Z)$ indicates $Y$ and $Z$ are the left and right subtrees, respectively, of node $X$. Note that $Y$ and $Z$ may be $NULL$, or further nested. Which of the following represents a valid binary tree?

  1. $(1 \ 2 \ (4 \ 5 \ 6 \ 7))$
  2. $(1 \ (2 \ 3 \ 4) \ 5 \ 6) \ 7)$
  3. $(1 \ (2 \ 3  \ 4) \ (5 \ 6  \ 7))$
  4. $(1 \ (2 \ 3 \ NULL) \ (4 \ 5))$

review.independentCheck: Binary tree 3-tuple notation requires (Root Left Right); Option C has (1 (2 3 4) (5 6 7)) where every nested subtree is a valid 3-tuple. Matches official key C.
review.notes: Binary tree 3-tuple notation requires (Root Left Right); Option C has (1 (2 3 4) (5 6 7)) where every nested subtree is a valid 3-tuple. Matches official key C.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 1.15
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
Let $S$ be a sorted array of $n$ integers. Let $T(n)$ denote the time taken for the most efficient algorithm to determined if there are two elements with sum less than $1000$ in $S$. Which of the following statement is true?

  1. $T (n)$ is $O(1)$
  2. $n \leq  T(n) \leq n \log_2 n$
  3. $n \log_2 n ≤ T(n) < \frac{n}{2}$
  4. $T(n) = \left (\frac{n}{2} \right)$

review.independentCheck: In a sorted array, the minimal pairwise sum is S[0] + S[1]; checking if S[0] + S[1] < 1000 takes O(1) time. Matches official key A.
review.notes: In a sorted array, the minimal pairwise sum is S[0] + S[1]; checking if S[0] + S[1] < 1000 takes O(1) time. Matches official key A.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 1.17, ISRO2015-79
questions.subject: Programming in C
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following C declaration:

struct {
    short x[5];  
    union { 
        float y; 
        long z; 
    } u;
 )t;

Assume that the objects of the type short, float and long occupy $2$ bytes, $4$ bytes and $8$ bytes, respectively. The memory requirement for variable $t$, ignoring alignment consideration, is:

  1. $22$ bytes
  2. $14$ bytes
  3. $18$ bytes
  4. $10$ bytes

review.independentCheck: Size of struct t = sizeof(short x[5]) + sizeof(union u) = (5*2) + max(4, 8) = 10 + 8 = 18 bytes. Matches official key C.
review.notes: Size of struct t = sizeof(short x[5]) + sizeof(union u) = (5*2) + max(4, 8) = 10 + 8 = 18 bytes. Matches official key C.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 1.21
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
Let $m[0]\ldots m[4]$ be mutexes (binary semaphores) and $P[0]\ldots P[4]$ be processes. 
Suppose each process $P[i]$ executes the following:

     wait (m[i]); wait (m(i+1) mod 4]);
     ........... 
     release (m[i]); release (m(i+1) mod 4]);

This could cause

  1. Thrashing
  2. Deadlock
  3. Starvation, but not deadlock
  4. None of the above

review.independentCheck: Circular resource acquisition wait(m[i]) followed by wait(m[(i+1) mod 4]) satisfies all 4 Coffman conditions, creating deadlock. Matches official key B.
review.notes: Circular resource acquisition wait(m[i]) followed by wait(m[(i+1) mod 4]) satisfies all 4 Coffman conditions, creating deadlock. Matches official key B.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.subject: Databases

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.19
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
Let $G$ be an undirected graph. Consider a depth-first traversal of $G$, and let $T$ be the resulting depth-first search tree. Let $u$ be a vertex in $G$ and let $v$ be the first new (unvisited) vertex visited after visiting $u$ in the traversal. Which of the following statement is always true?

  1. $\{u, v\}$ must be an edge in $G$, and $u$ is a descendant of $v$ in $T$
  2. $\{u, v\}$ must be an edge in $G$, and $v$ is a descendant of $u$ in $T$
  3. If $\{u, v\}$ is not an edge in $G$ then $u$ is a leaf in $T$
  4. If $\{u, v\}$ is not an edge in $G$ then $u$ and $v$ must have the same parent in $T$

review.independentCheck: If {u, v} is not an edge in G, DFS backtracked from u before finding unvisited v from an ancestor, proving u had no unvisited neighbors and is a leaf in T. Matches official key C.
review.notes: If {u, v} is not an edge in G, DFS backtracked from u before finding unvisited v from an ancestor, proving u had no unvisited neighbors and is a leaf in T. Matches official key C.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.8
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.questionHtml:
What can be said about a regular language L over {a} whose minimal finite state automaton has two states?

  1. L must be $\{a^n \mid n \ \text{ is odd}\}$
  2. L must be $\{a^n \mid n \ \text{ is even}\}$
  3. L must be $\{a^n \mid n \geq 0\}$
  4. Either L must be$\{a^n \mid n \text{ is odd}\}$, or L must be $\{a^n \mid n \text{ is even}\}$

review.independentCheck: A 2-state minimal DFA over unary alphabet {a} without dead states forms a mod-2 alternating cycle, accepting either all odd-length strings or all even-length strings. Matches official key D.
review.notes: A 2-state minimal DFA over unary alphabet {a} without dead states forms a mod-2 alternating cycle, accepting either all odd-length strings or all even-length strings. Matches official key D.
review.answerKeySource: Existing UID answer record cross-checked against the displayed question/options and independent derivation; no answer key changed.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.10
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
The simultaneous equations on the Boolean variables $x, y, z$ and $w$,

  • $x + y + z = 1 $
  • $xy = 0$
  • $xz + w = 1$
  • $xy + \bar{z}\bar{w} = 0$

have the following solution for $x, y, z$ and $w,$ respectively:

  1. $0 \ 1 \ 0 \ 0$
  2. $1 \ 1 \ 0 \ 1$
  3. $1 \ 0 \ 1 \ 1$
  4. $1 \ 0 \ 0 \ 0$

review.independentCheck: Simultaneous Boolean equations solved algebraically: xy=0 and xy+~z~w=0 gives z+w=1; (1, 0, 1, 1) satisfies all 4 equations. Matches official key C.
review.notes: Simultaneous Boolean equations solved algebraically: xy=0 and xy+~z~w=0 gives z+w=1; (1, 0, 1, 1) satisfies all 4 equations. Matches official key C.
